records.name: Bayelsa
records.current_summary: No regional protective statute, recorded incident series or documented enforcement divergence from the national framework has been documented for this state. The national framework applies in full: a 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and — as reported in August 2026 summarising a foreign government's travel advisory — also reaches assisting, attending or promoting same-sex ceremonies and LGBT+ organisations; religious criminal law in some northern states can carry the death penalty for same-sex conduct. The same advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to this country of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation.  The recorded violence pattern is national and recent: a 33-year-old transgender media personality and sex worker was beaten to death in the federal capital in August 2024, having reported a stabbing a year earlier and said she feared for her life; authorities ordered a discreet investigation. sources.claim: Sahara Reporters (19 Aug 2026): the UK FCDO travel advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation - same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years' imprisonment federally; some northern states operate Sharia law where it can carry the death penalty; the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also criminalises participants and guests at same-sex weddings.

Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916 and that the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act — passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014 — criminalises all forms of same-sex unions, rendering any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. It states the maximum penalty under federal law is up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the death penalty confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, and that in the southern portion of the country, which includes Bayelsa, the maximum punishment for same-sex sexual activity is 14 years' imprisonment. The page also records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. This is the national-framework source for the record's claim that the 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions in Bayelsa with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note on Nigeria documents the national criminal framework on sexual orientation and gender identity that applies across all states, including the 2014 statute punishing same-sex unions, and records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. It confirms that the twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes — with penalties for same-sex conduct from lashes or caning up to death by stoning — remain in force, citing a Shari'a court in Bauchi sentencing three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, a further report of a death-by-stoning sentence from Bauchi in May 2024, and a January 2014 incident in which a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial. This confirms that the death-penalty risk layer is confined to the northern Shari'a states and does not extend to southern states such as Bayelsa, which stands under the secular national 14-year framework — matching this record's position that no state-specific enforcement divergence is documented.

It documents that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after the Act, including eight of the 21 young men arrested, but never charged, at a birthday party in Ibadan, and - relevant to Rivers State itself - the case of Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos who in January 2015 travelled to Port Harcourt to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there, saying he did not report it to the police. The named Port Harcourt incident and the nationwide abuse pattern substantiate the enforcement climate a same-sex couple or trans visitor faces in Rivers.
